bull_bear.title: Management commentary

bull_bear.body:
- **GRM volatility** — refining margins swing with crude–product spreads and global supply/demand.
- **Marketing-margin / pricing risk** — auto-fuel marketing margins can compress when retail prices lag crude spikes (administered-pricing / political sensitivity for a PSU OMC).
- **Subsidy / LPG under-recovery** — domestic LPG (and any cooking-fuel under-recovery) can weigh on cash flows pending government compensation.
- **Leverage from large capex + working capital** — sizeable refinery/petchem/transition capex plus crude-inventory and receivable working-capital swings pressure debt and coverage.
- **Energy-transition risk** — long-run demand shift away from fossil transport fuels; execution risk on green-H2/EV/biofuel investments.
- **FX / crude price** — foreign-currency borrowing and crude import dependence expose IOC to rupee and oil-price moves.
bull_bear.title: Key risks

business.body:
Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOC / "IndianOil") is India's largest integrated oil & gas company and a Maharatna PSU majority-owned by the Government of India. It operates across the full downstream value chain: crude refining, petroleum-product marketing (fuel retail + bulk/industrial + LPG/aviation), a large cross-country pipeline network, petrochemicals, natural gas, and an expanding new-energy portfolio (green hydrogen, EV charging, biofuels/ethanol, batteries). It is the flagship national oil-marketing company (OMC) alongside BPCL and HPCL.

risks.note: Geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, sanctions and disruptions across critical energy corridors influence global energy markets. Developments in West Asia and around the Strait of Hormuz - through which nearly 20% of global oil and LNG trade flows - drove volatility across crude oil, natural gas, freight and insurance markets. The Directors' Report states directly that despite excellent FY26 performance, 'escalation of geopolitical disruptions may have an adverse impact on profitability of 2026-27', and that the fag end of 2025-26 saw prolonged disruptions to the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz and significant dislocations in global supply chains for petroleum products and LPG.
risks.risk: Rising geopolitical risk and disruption of critical energy corridors

risks.note: India's crude oil import dependence has increased to around 88%, and growing gas demand is expected to raise LNG import requirements over the medium term. Dependence on imported crude oil, LNG, petrochemical feedstocks and critical minerals exposes the business to supply concentration risk, currency fluctuation and external market disruption - raising the importance of diversified sourcing, resilient logistics and long-term supply arrangements. Crude sourcing, supply-chain continuity and foreign exchange exposure are named as key risks the Company actively managed during the year.
risks.risk: High import dependence and supply-security concentration

risks.note: Global energy markets are increasingly characterised by short-term price volatility rather than stable pricing cycles. The correction in India's gas consumption during H1 2025-26, driven by elevated LNG spot prices, demonstrated how sensitive demand is to commodity prices. Such volatility influences procurement strategies, inventory management, project economics and capital-allocation decisions - directly relevant for a company whose refining margins are also listed among the key risks managed during the year.
risks.risk: Energy price volatility and margin uncertainty

risks.note: Large-scale petrochemical capacity additions in China and the Middle East continue to pressure global utilisation rates and margins. Naphtha-based producers - which is IndianOil's position - remain exposed to feedstock cost volatility and to competition from gas-based producers benefiting from lower-cost ethane and LPG feedstocks. Prolonged oversupply may continue to affect profitability across commodity petrochemical value chains, a structural headwind against the Company's petrochemical expansion strategy.
risks.risk: Petrochemical margin pressure from global oversupply

risks.note: The energy transition brings stricter environmental regulations, carbon-related trade measures, fuel-quality requirements and disclosure obligations. Emerging frameworks on emissions, carbon intensity, sustainable fuels, shipping and industrial decarbonisation may increase compliance requirements, affect competitiveness and require additional investment in cleaner technologies and operating systems.

Increasing frequency and intensity of heatwaves, floods and other climate events present operational and infrastructure risks across the energy value chain. Rising cooling-driven electricity demand, pressure on power systems and weather-related disruptions increase the need for resilient infrastructure, storage and operational flexibility; rapid renewable expansion also requires continued investment in transmission, balancing mechanisms and grid stability.

Regional supply alliances, export controls, sanctions and strategic competition across energy technologies may alter trade flows, investment patterns and technology access. Separately, the shift toward batteries, renewables, electrolysers, semiconductors and digital infrastructure increases dependence on critical minerals whose global supply chains (lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths, batteries, clean-energy equipment) remain highly concentrated geographically - a new form of strategic vulnerability, trade risk and price uncertainty for IndianOil's transition investments.
risks.risk: Changing global trade flows, emerging energy blocs and critical-mineral / technology supply-chain dependence

risks.note: This is a company-specific structural risk disclosed in the Directors' Report itself. The Company has an ERM framework and constituted a Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board, but 'due to non-availability of any Independent Director on the Board, the RMC has been discontinued w.e.f. March 28, 2026', as was the Audit Committee. Board-level risk oversight now rests on the management-level Risk Management Compliance Board (senior management personnel headed by the Chief Risk Officer), because changes to the Risk Register require RMC approval and periodic updates go to the Audit Committee and Board. Appointment of directors vests with the Government of India through MoP&NG, so remediation is outside the Company's control.
